title: Abstraction Inversion
pattern: An interface exposes only extremely low-level, primitive methods, forcing all of its callers to build high-level common-case operations themselves, duplicating effort.
why_bad: It turns the interface inside out. Instead of the abstraction hiding complexity, it forces the caller to write boilerplate wrapper loops, leading to duplicated and poorly optimized code.
detection: Callers repeatedly implementing the same high-level helper functions using the exposed low-level primitives of an interface.
counterexample: Extremely minimal hardware-level drivers where keeping the abstraction layer light is necessary for safety-critical memory budgets.
fix: Build the common-case, high-level operations directly into the interface or a standard utility layer alongside the low-level API (e.g., providing `read_line` directly).
source: John K. Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design* (2018), Chapter 4 ("Deep Modules" / Abstraction Inversion); Benjamin C. Pierce, *Types and Programming Languages* (2002), Chapter 24.
